results.summary: This project implements the Intel MCS-4 4004 CPU in Verilog, intended for use in a replica of the 141-PF calculator. The design can be configured in three ways: as an internal CPU within an FPGA, as an FPGA-based CPU connected to external MCS-4 system components, or as a standalone chip connected to an FPGA-based MCS-4 system. The chip requires external ROM and RAM to function as a complete system, and the documentation describes a debug system using an FPGA and a RISC-V subsystem for chip selection. The design is notable for being a faithful reproduction of a historical microprocessor, but the documentation is somewhat sparse on specific implementation details and testing procedures.

This project is a simple test design for Tiny Tapeout, with eight input pins and eight output pins. The documentation states that it works by trial and error and was tested with APyTypes, but provides no further details on its function or purpose. It appears to be a minimal or template design with essentially no documentation. The design is not intended for any specific application beyond testing the shuttle process.

This project implements a minimal RISC-style processor with an FSM-based control unit, supporting LOAD, ADD, SUB, and STORE instructions. Instructions are provided via the ui_in pins, and the accumulator value or operation result is output on uo_out. The design is intended for educational purposes, demonstrating how a simple processor can be built and tested. It can be tested in simulation with Icarus Verilog and cocotb, and on hardware using a Raspberry Pi to send instructions and observe outputs. The documentation is clear and provides a testbench and testing procedure.

This project implements a 3-bit modulo-6 synchronous counter that increments on each clock rising edge and wraps from 5 to 0. The counter value is output on uo_out[2:0], with higher bits tied to zero. It has an active-low asynchronous reset and no other inputs. The design can be tested using cocotb or Verilog testbenches, and is a simple educational example of a counter. The documentation is clear and complete.

This project is a mini MOSbius analog chip in a 3x2 tile slot, containing programmable NMOS and PMOS transistors, differential pairs, a 5T-OTA, and current sources. It includes six buses, five of which connect to external pins, and 196 transmission gates for interconnecting blocks, programmed via a shift register. The chip requires a 100uA bias current and a digital pattern generator to program the shift register. Silicon test reports indicate it is working, with tests on inverter, diff amp, ring oscillator, and current sources. The design is notable for being a flexible analog prototyping platform, though the programming file generation is still a work in progress.

This project is an 8-bit custom processor with a program counter, control unit, ALU, and register file. It fetches instructions, decodes them, performs operations via the ALU, and stores results, all synchronized with the clock. The ALU output is available on uo_out. The design can be tested using a cocotb testbench provided in the test folder. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic architecture and testing approach.

This project implements Conway's Game of Life with VGA output and GPIO controls for field manipulation and randomization. It uses a 2x2 tile area and outputs VGA signals on uo_out, with bidirectional pins for selection and control. The design includes features like free-run divisor, external hold, and step, and supports randomizing the field. It requires a Tiny VGA PMOD for display. The documentation is clear and provides pin descriptions and recommended pinout.

RISCY Jr. is an original 8-bit microcontroller design with SPI, UART, PWM, and PRNG peripherals. It uses an external RP2040 for SPI RAM emulation and supports UART with optional hardware flow control. The design includes GPIO, external hold/step, and a CPU activity indicator. It is intended for embedded applications and can be tested with standard SPI and UART interfaces. The documentation is detailed and provides pinouts and external hardware requirements.

This project adds retro VGA graphics to existing Tiny Tapeout projects by using their 7-segment display outputs as input. It outputs VGA signals on uo_out and accepts 7-segment segment signals on ui_in. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and can potentially synchronize with the source circuit via VSYNC. Silicon test reports indicate it is working, with a default 'HELLO 3OrLd' message and acceptance of other inputs. The design is notable for its creative reuse of existing projects and was submitted for the VGA Demoscene.

This project is a 2x2 OpenFPGA fabric with 4 configurable logic blocks, 8 I/O blocks, 9 switch boxes, and 12 connection boxes. It can be configured with a bitstream to implement user-defined digital circuits, with inputs and outputs via the I/O blocks. The design can be tested by loading a bitstream and driving inputs, observing outputs with lab equipment. No dedicated peripherals are required, but standard lab equipment may be used for evaluation. The documentation is clear and describes the architecture and testing approach.
